etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English profit, from Old French profit (Modern French profit), from Latin prōfectus (“advance, progress, growth, increase, profit”), from proficiō (“to go forward, advance, make progress, be profitable or useful”). Doublet of profect.

definitions.definition: (accounting, economics) Total income or cash flow minus expenditures. The money or other benefit a non-governmental organization or individual receives in exchange for products and services sold at an advertised price.

quote.text: Let no man anticipate uncertain profits.

quote.citation: 1935, Smedley Butler, War Is a Racket, page 1 & 7:
quote.text: War is a racket. It always has been. It is possibly the oldest, easily the most profitable, surely the most vicious. It is the only one international in scope. It is the only one in which the profits are reckoned in dollars and the losses in lives... Of course, it isn't put that crudely in war time. It is dressed into speeches about patriotism, love of country, and "we must all put our shoulders to the wheel," but the profits jump and leap and skyrocket—and are safely pocketed.

quote.citation: 2013 June 22, “T time”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8841, page 68:
quote.text: The ability to shift profits to low-tax countries by locating intellectual property in them, which is then licensed to related businesses in high-tax countries, is often assumed to be the preserve of high-tech companies. […] current tax rules make it easy for all sorts of firms to generate […] “stateless income”: profit subject to tax in a jurisdiction that is neither the location of the factors of production that generate the income nor where the parent firm is domiciled.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Corinthians vii:35:
quote.text: This I speak for your own profit.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: if you dare do yourself a profit and a right

definitions.definition: (property law) Ellipsis of profit à prendre.
(transitive) To benefit (somebody), be of use to (somebody).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Hebrews 4:2:
quote.text: The word preached did not profit them.

quote.citation: 1695, C[harles] A[lphonse] du Fresnoy, translated by John Dryden, De Arte Graphica. The Art of Painting, […], London:  […]  J[ohn] Heptinstall for W. Rogers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: It is a great means of profiting yourself, to copy diligently those excellent pieces and beautiful designs.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, construed with from) To benefit, gain.
(intransitive, construed with from) To take advantage of, exploit, use.
